strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated gap: existing EEG foundation models lack a fully discretized tokenizer (unlike NLP/vision), and existing approaches suffer from frequency-representation collapse and reliance on cross-channel prediction. The single-channel, time-frequency-based tokenization angle is sensible and clearly positioned.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four established EEG benchmarks (TUEV, TUAB, IIIC, CHB-MIT) with five random seeds, standard metrics (balanced accuracy, Cohen's Kappa, weighted F1, AUC-PR, AUROC), and reproduced open-source baselines including recent SOTA models (BIOT, LaBraM).

The tokenizer-swap experiment (Table 3), showing that replacing LaBraM's neural tokenizer with TFM-Tokenizer improves performance, is a valuable control that directly tests whether the learned tokens (rather than architecture or training procedure) drive the gains.

Unusually thorough ablation studies: tokenizer variants (raw-only, STFT-only, joint), masking strategies (random vs. frequency-bin vs. temporal vs. symmetric), positional embedding removal, vocabulary size, and masked-token-prediction pretraining. The finding that removing positional encodings improves token quality is an interesting and well-analyzed empirical insight.

Token quality analysis goes beyond accuracy: token utilization, class-token uniqueness, retrieval-based mining, spectral entropy analysis, and qualitative visualization of motifs (Figure 5) provide evidence that the learned tokens are compact, class-distinctive, and interpretable. The model also achieves results with substantially fewer parameters than LaBraM.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter tables, STFT configurations, dataset statistics, and split protocols are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: A central claimed contribution—'scalable tokenization' adaptable across channel configurations, devices, and tasks—is not directly validated. All experiments are in a single-dataset, 16-channel fixed-montage setting. There are no cross-dataset, cross-montage, or variable-channel generalization experiments (e.g., training on 16 channels and testing on 1–2 channel setups), so the scalability/generalization claims in the motivation and contributions are stronger than the evidence.

All pretraining is done on the downstream dataset itself ('single-dataset setting'). This undercuts the foundation-model framing: the paper's motivation criticizes case-by-case models, yet the evaluation paradigm is essentially case-by-case with an extra pretraining stage. A cross-task or cross-corpus pretraining experiment would substantially strengthen the claims.

Novelty is moderate: the method is a fairly natural combination of known components (VQ-VAE, STFT patching, masked reconstruction, linear attention from Linformer/Katharopoulos). The joint frequency-temporal masking and gated patchwise aggregation are reasonable but incremental refinements.

The interpretability study (Q4, Figure 5) is purely qualitative visual inspection by the authors, without quantitative metrics or expert (clinician) evaluation. Claims that tokens 'may capture clinically useful patterns' remain speculative.

Some internal inconsistencies and overstatements: Table 7 shows temporal masking degrades Cohen's Kappa relative to frequency-bin masking alone (0.5193 → 0.5045), which complicates the joint-modeling narrative; percent improvements in the text (e.g., '5% improvement in balanced accuracy') sometimes conflate relative and absolute gains; several typos ('Scable', 'learnbale', 'Frequency Making Prediction', 'Abnoral') suggest insufficient polish.

Token utilization/utilization-gap analyses are somewhat ad hoc: lower utilization is presented as a benefit, but the relationship between utilization, uniqueness, and downstream utility is not established, and the Class-Token Uniqueness metric is introduced without external validation.

Gains on TUAB over the strongest baselines are modest (e.g., ~2 points balanced accuracy over BIOT/ST-Transformer) and confidence intervals overlap for some comparisons; no statistical significance testing is reported despite five seeds.

The comparison to LaBraM at its published channel setting is acknowledged but the fairness of single-dataset LaBraM reproduction (a model designed for large-scale cross-corpus pretraining) could be challenged; LaBraM's notably poor CHB-MIT results (AUC-PR 0.096) suggest possible reproduction/suboptimality issues.

strengths: Clear and well-structured problem formulation: the paper explicitly separates the tokenization problem (Problem Statement 1) from the downstream classification problem (Problem Statement 2), and the motivation for single-channel, fully discretized tokenization is clearly articulated.

Comprehensive evaluation on four standard EEG benchmarks (TUEV, TUAB, IIIC Seizure, CHB-MIT) with appropriate metrics (balanced accuracy, Cohen's Kappa, weighted F1, AUC-PR, AUROC) and five random seeds, outperforming recent strong baselines (BIOT, LaBraM) with fewer parameters.

The paper goes beyond raw accuracy: token utilization, class-token uniqueness, retrieval, spectral entropy analysis, and qualitative motif visualization provide meaningful evidence about token quality and interpretability.

Several useful ablations are included (joint vs. single-domain modeling, masking strategies, vocabulary size, position embeddings, masked token prediction), and limitations of fixed windowing are honestly acknowledged.
The finding that removing positional encodings improves token learning is an interesting empirical observation with a plausible neurophysiological rationale.
The method is plug-compatible with existing foundation models: swapping LaBraM's neural tokenizer with TFM-Tokenizer improves performance, demonstrating practical utility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core method is essentially a VQ-VAE applied to STFT + raw-signal patch features with band/temporal masking. Each ingredient (VQ-VAE, STFT-based features, masked reconstruction, linear attention, gated aggregation) is standard; the combination is reasonable but incremental for a top-tier AI venue.

The evaluation undermines the central scalability/generalization claims. The introduction motivates the work by cross-task, cross-channel, and cross-format generalization, yet all experiments (including tokenizer and encoder pretraining) are conducted in a single-dataset setting with a fixed 16-channel bipolar montage. There are no cross-dataset transfer or variable-channel-configuration experiments to support the headline 'scalable tokenization' claim.

Reported improvements are partly overstated: the abstract claims '5% improvement' in balanced accuracy, but 0.4679 to 0.4943 is a 2.6-point absolute gain (the text conflates absolute and relative percentages). With large reported variances (e.g., LaBraM ±0.0856 on TUEV; TFM-Token ±0.0516), no statistical significance testing is provided, making some gaps between the top methods hard to interpret.

Ablation results are internally inconsistent and only partially explained: TFM-Token-S beats TFM-Token-R on Cohen's Kappa but loses on AUC-PR for TUAB, and the masking ablation shows frequency+temporal masking degrading Kappa/F1 until symmetric masking is added—suggesting the gains may be sensitive to specific configuration choices rather than a robust property of joint time-frequency modeling.

The interpretability analysis (Section 5.5) is anecdotal: a handful of hand-selected tokens on two classes, with no quantitative or human-subject validation of motif correspondence. The class-token uniqueness metric is novel but not validated against any ground truth of what 'class-specific' motifs should be.

The CHB-MIT split (fixed subjects 1-19/20-21/22-23) is small and the AUC-PR of all baselines below 0.25 except BIOT raises questions about whether this benchmark is meaningfully evaluated; similarly, LaBraM's poor CHB-MIT results (AUROC 0.66) may indicate suboptimal baseline reproduction rather than a genuine advantage of the proposed method.

Presentation issues: several typos and inconsistencies ('Scable tokenization', 'TFM-Token' vs 'TFM-Tokenizer' naming, 'learnbale', 'i.e.g', 'Frequency Making Prediction' presumably 'Masking', 'Abnoral' in Table 11) and an inconsistent loss notation (L_rec vs L_recon) reduce polish.

Writing implies foundation-model ambitions (pretraining techniques from NLP, enhancing foundation models) but no large-scale pretraining or evaluation of the cross-corpus setting that would justify this framing.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies concrete limitations of existing EEG foundation models (non-discrete tokenization, frequency representation collapse, channel-dependence) and targets each one directly.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four standard EEG benchmarks (TUEV, TUAB, CHB-MIT, IIIC) with five random seeds, appropriate metrics (balanced accuracy, Cohen's Kappa, weighted-F1, AUC-PR, AUROC), and consistent SOTA results across all tasks.

Unusually thorough ablation studies: masking strategies (Table 7), position embeddings (Table 6), vocabulary size (Figs. 7-8), masked token prediction (Fig. 6), and tokenizer variants (raw-only, STFT-only, joint), which support the design choices rather than just the final system.

Beyond accuracy, the token-quality analyses (token utilization, class-token uniqueness, retrieval with Jaccard similarity, spectral entropy, and qualitative motif visualization in Fig. 5) provide meaningful evidence that the learned discrete tokens are interpretable and class-discriminative.

Demonstrates plug-and-play utility: replacing LaBraM's neural tokenizer with TFM-Tokenizer improves its performance (Table 3), supporting the claim that the tokenizer can enhance existing foundation models.
Efficiency: achieves the best results with ~1.9M parameters, a 3-fold reduction over LaBraM, which is practically relevant for clinical deployment.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core components (VQ-VAE quantization, STFT features, masked prediction, linear attention, gated aggregation) are all established; the contribution is primarily their combination and adaptation to EEG, which is incremental.

The central claims of scalability and generalization are not directly tested. All pretraining and evaluation are done in a single-dataset setting; there are no cross-dataset transfer, cross-montage, or variable-channel-configuration experiments, despite these being the main motivations (Section 1) and the basis of the title.
Single-dataset pretraining somewhat undermines the 'foundation model' framing; a tokenizer trained on one dataset and tested on another would much more convincingly support the generalization claims.

Some results are mixed or have high variance that weakens the claims: e.g., TFM-Token's TUEV balanced accuracy has std ±0.0516 (larger than some margins over baselines), and TFM-Token-R beats the full model on TUAB AUC-PR in Table 1, complicating the 'joint modeling is necessary' narrative.

The proposed Class-Token Uniqueness metric and the Jaccard-based retrieval protocol are novel but unvalidated against external ground truth; the authors themselves acknowledge that 'further research is needed to identify optimal metrics for token-based EEG retrieval.'

Writing quality issues throughout: repeated typos ('Scable tokenization', 'Frequency Making Prediction', 'learnbale', 'i.e.g', 'Abnoral'), and inconsistent naming (TFM-Token vs. TFM-Token-izer vs. TFM-Token-izer-R/S) distract from the content.

Acknowledged but unresolved limitation: fixed windowing splits distinct EEG patterns across adjacent windows, assigning them separate tokens — a non-trivial failure mode for a motif-based tokenizer that is only mentioned in passing.

No mention of code release, and hyperparameters were tuned via a lengthy three-phase search on the same datasets used for evaluation, raising mild fairness questions relative to baselines with their default configurations.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies a genuine gap—existing EEG foundation models either use fixed segment-based tokenization or use learned tokenizers only as training objectives—and positions discrete, reusable token inputs as a meaningful contribution.

Technically sensible design: the dual-path (spectral + temporal) encoding with a Localized Spectral Window Encoder, gated patchwise aggregation, frequency-band masking, and VQ codebook is a coherent solution to the stated challenges (motif robustness, frequency resolution, tokenization objective). The ablation on removing position embeddings is a nice, empirically supported insight for non-stationary signals.

Broad empirical evaluation: four EEG benchmarks (TUEV, TUAB, IIIC, CHB-MIT) plus an out-of-domain ear-EEG sleep staging experiment (EESM23), two experimental regimes (single- and multi-dataset pretraining), and plug-and-play integration with BIOT and LaBraM. Consistent improvements across settings, with a lightweight (~0.7M) downstream model.

Token quality analyses (class-token uniqueness, retrieval-based consistency, spectral entropy of token sequences, qualitative motif visualization in Figure 5) go beyond raw accuracy and support the central claim that learned tokens are class-discriminative and frequency-aware.

Strong reproducibility: code and pretrained weights promised, detailed hyperparameters (Ray Tune/Optuna tuning procedure, STFT parameters, architecture tables), multiple seeds with mean±std reported, and a masking-strategy ablation.
Honest reporting of limitations (e.g., windowing artifacts in Section 4.7, non-monotonic vocabulary-size effects) and acknowledgment that LaBraM was retrained on smaller corpora for fairness.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison fairness is the main concern: several headline gains (up to 17% Cohen's Kappa on TUEV, 36% on IIIC) are measured against reproduced baselines (BIOT*, LaBraM*) trained only within the paper's four-dataset corpora, whereas the original LaBraM was pretrained on 2,500+ hours. The paper acknowledges this, but the reported margins over the *published* state of the art are considerably smaller, weakening the significance claims.

Novelty is incremental at the component level: VQ-VAE codebooks, masked spectral modeling, dual-path frequency/temporal encoders, and gated aggregation are all established techniques (VQ-VAE, LaBraM/BEiT-style masking, frequency-domain time-series models). The contribution is primarily a well-engineered combination and the single-channel tokenization framing rather than a fundamentally new method.

The ear-EEG scalability result is on only 10 subjects (~8K training samples) with modest absolute gaps (e.g., 0.3883 vs. 0.3406 Kappa vs. LaBraM), so the cross-device scalability claim, while plausible, rests on limited evidence.

Some analyses are exploratory or underdeveloped: token consistency via Jaccard similarity is acknowledged as needing better metrics; token utilization drops (21% -> 9.8%), which could indicate codebook underuse but is framed purely positively; several ablation differences are within or near one standard deviation without significance tests.

Only three random seeds per experiment; statistical significance is reported for only one comparison (EESM23, p=0.02), not for the main benchmark tables where several gaps are small (e.g., TUAB improvements are within ~0.5-1%).

Positioning versus recent EEG tokenization/discretization work (e.g., DeWave and other VQ-based EEG approaches) could be deepened; the related-work comparison to learned tokenizers is mostly limited to LaBraM's internal tokenizer.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and well-motivated problem: learning a discrete token vocabulary for single-channel EEG that can serve as a reusable interface for foundation models, with clear articulation of the three key challenges (tokenization target, resolution, and learning objective).

The dual-path time-frequency encoding with gated patchwise aggregation and joint frequency/temporal masking is a reasonable technical design, and the ablation studies (input representation, masking strategy, vocabulary size, position embeddings, number of downstream layers) are fairly thorough.

Evaluation spans four EEG benchmarks plus an out-of-domain ear-EEG sleep staging setting, and includes both standalone and plug-and-play experiments with BIOT and LaBraM, along with qualitative token/motif visualizations.
A reproducibility statement, released code/weights, and detailed hyperparameter appendices improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and largely incremental: the core components are standard—VQ-VAE codebooks, STFT spectrogram inputs, masked modeling, and dual-path/frequency-aware architectures that are well established in time-series and speech work. The claim of being 'the first to investigate single-channel EEG tokenization' feels overstated given prior VQ-based EEG discretization (e.g., Duan et al. 2023) and LaBraM's neural tokenizer.

Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: LaBraM is 'reproduced' with only four datasets of pretraining instead of its original 2,500-hour corpus, and BIOT is reproduced rather than using its best variant, while headline gains (17% on TUEV) come from the multi-dataset setting where these weakened baselines are compared. The strongest claims rest on potentially under-tuned or under-trained reproduced baselines rather than official results.

Some reported improvements are inconsistent or modest across settings—e.g., LaBraM-TFM degrades Balanced Accuracy relative to LaBraM on TUEV (single: 0.5147 vs 0.4682 is a gain, but multiple: 0.5541 vs 0.5550 is a loss) and on CHB-MIT AUROC—yet the text claims consistent gains of 'at least 3% in most cases', which oversells the evidence.

Token quality metrics (class-token uniqueness, utilization, Jaccard-based retrieval precision) are ad hoc, and the authors themselves concede 'further work is needed to identify optimal metrics'; these analyses support plausibility rather than rigorously validating the central 'motif' claim.

The motif interpretability analysis is qualitative and limited to a few hand-picked tokens from one dataset; no quantitative evidence that tokens align with neurophysiologically defined motifs beyond anecdotal examples, and the fixed-window limitation is acknowledged but unaddressed.

Statistical significance reporting is sparse; only the ear-EEG comparison reports a p-value, and error bars come from three seeds, which is thin for the magnitude of claims (e.g., '36% improvement' on IIIC).

Significance of the contribution is unclear: it remains to be demonstrated that discrete tokenization actually delivers benefits over continuous segment-level embeddings beyond the specific reproduced baselines—for example, no experiments on generative or cross-modal downstream tasks that discrete tokens would uniquely enable, which would justify the tokenization framing.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies a genuine gap in EEG foundation modeling (learned discrete tokenization of raw signals as model inputs, rather than a discarded training objective), and formulates the single-channel tokenization problem precisely in Appendix A.

Technically sensible design: the dual-path spectral/temporal encoding with gated patchwise aggregation and frequency-band masking is a reasonable and well-argued solution to the stated challenges (motif robustness, time-frequency entanglement), and omitting positional encodings is a defensible, empirically validated choice.

Broad and mostly convincing evaluation: four EEG benchmarks plus an out-of-domain ear-EEG sleep staging test, comparisons against multiple recent baselines (BIOT, LaBraM, EEGPT, NeuroLM) under both single- and multi-dataset pretraining, and plug-and-play integration with two foundation models.

Extensive ablations and analyses: token encoder variants, masking strategies, vocabulary size, depth, position embeddings, masked-token-prediction pretraining, cross-dataset token generalization, and qualitative motif visualization — the appendix is thorough and mostly supports the claims.
Reproducibility: code, pretrained weights, full hyperparameter tables, and systematic hyperparameter tuning procedures are provided; seeds and mean±std over three runs are reported.
weaknesses: The headline 17% improvement comes from comparing against a reproduced LaBraM* trained only on four datasets (8.6M-tokenizer variant), while the original LaBraM was pretrained on 2,500+ hours; absolute gains over the strongest published foundation-model numbers are smaller and less uniform, so the magnitude of the contribution is somewhat overstated in the abstract/intro.

Plug-and-play gains on foundation models are modest (roughly 3-4% in most cases, and one direction on CHB-MIT actually degrades AUC-PR for LaBraM+TFM in the multi-dataset setting), which weakens the 'consistently boosts' claim; statistical significance is rarely reported (only p=0.02 for the ear-EEG experiment).

Component novelty is limited: VQ-VAE quantization, dual encoders, masked reconstruction, and symmetric masking are all standard techniques; the contribution is primarily an application/domain-specific combination rather than a new methodological idea, and the related-work claim of being 'the first' to tokenize single-channel EEG into time-frequency motifs should be softened given prior VQ-based EEG work (e.g., Duan et al. 2023).

Some token-quality metrics feel ad hoc and weakly validated: class-token uniqueness, Jaccard-based retrieval precision, and spectral-entropy analyses lack ground-truth grounding (the authors themselves acknowledge 'further work is needed to identify optimal metrics'), and the interpretation of these metrics (e.g., low utilization as a virtue) is debatable.

Fairness concerns in comparisons: EEGPT results are taken from published numbers on some datasets and fine-tuned on others, and baseline hyperparameter tuning budgets relative to the proposed method are not fully described; a few tables show large standard deviations overlapping between methods.

Minor clarity issues: the missing repository URL in the abstract/reproducibility statement ('Code is available at'), the fixed-window limitation acknowledged in Sec 4.7 is not addressed, and the relationship between tokenizer pretraining corpus and evaluation data in cross-dataset experiments could be stated more carefully to rule out leakage.
